summary: RFC 7830 defines the EDNS(0) Padding option but not how much to pad. This experimental memo lists possible padding policies, discusses their implications, and recommends one option.

plainLanguage.summary: When DNS traffic is encrypted, the size of each message can still give away what was asked. This RFC says how much extra space to add to each DNS message so that the sizes reveal less, and explains why the simplest choices, such as always padding to the maximum, are a poor idea.

questions: how much to pad dns messages
how much should dns messages be padded
what is block length padding for dns
subtitle: How much to pad encrypted DNS messages so their sizes reveal less.

tldr.problem: The EDNS(0) Padding option lets a DNS client or server enlarge a DNS message, but RFC 7830 deliberately leaves the amount of padding to the implementer, and padding the wrong amount can leak the original message size.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends Block-Length Padding: pad queries to a multiple of 128 octets and responses to a multiple of 468 octets, a policy derived from empirical work on real DNS traffic.
tldr.outcome: It also lists the strategies that are not recommended, including maximal-length padding and random-length padding, and warns that padding does not stop side channels such as timing.

today: RFC 8467 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document notes that the recommended strategy may need to be revisited once DNSSEC-validating clients become more prevalent and the observed size patterns change.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7830 specifies the Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0)) Padding option, which allows DNS clients and servers to artificially increase the size of a DNS message by a variable number of bytes, hampering size-based correlation of encrypted DNS messages.

RFC 7830 deliberately does not specify the actual length of padding to be used. This document discusses options regarding the actual size of padding, lists the advantages and disadvantages of each of these padding strategies, and provides a recommended, experimental strategy.

Padding DNS messages is useful only when the transport is encrypted, using protocols such as DNS over Transport Layer Security (RFC 7858), DNS over Datagram Transport Layer Security (RFC 8094), or other encrypted DNS transports specified in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: When DNS traffic is encrypted, the size of each message can still give away what was asked. This RFC says how much extra space to add to each DNS message so that the sizes reveal less, and explains why the simplest choices, such as always padding to the maximum, are a poor idea.

sections.title: General Guidance
sections.content:
Three constraints shape any padding policy.

The first is the EDNS(0) options space. The maximum message length, as dictated by the protocol, limits the space for EDNS(0) options. Since padding reduces the message space available to other EDNS(0) options, the Padding option MUST be the last EDNS(0) option applied before a DNS message is sent.

The second is resource conservation. Especially in situations where networking and processing resources are scarce, for example battery-powered long-life devices, low bandwidth or high-cost links, the trade-off between the increased size of padded DNS messages and the corresponding gain in confidentiality must be carefully considered.

The third is transport protocol independence. The message size used as input to the various padding strategies MUST be calculated excluding the potential extra 2-octet length field used in TCP transport. Otherwise, the padded, observable size of the DNS packets could significantly change between different transport protocols and reveal an indication of the original, unpadded length. The document's example is a Block-Length Padding strategy with a block length of 32 octets and a DNS message of 59 octets, which would be padded to 64 octets over UDP. If the same message were transported over TCP and the padding strategy counted the extra 2 octets of the length field, making 61 octets in total, the padded message would be 96 octets long, since the minimum length of the Padding option is 4 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things constrain any padding policy. The padding must not squeeze out other options, it must not cost more than the privacy gain is worth on a small device or a slow link, and it must give the same result over UDP and over TCP so that the transport itself does not leak the original size.

sections.title: The Recommended Strategy: Block-Length Padding
sections.content:
Based on empirical research performed by Daniel K. Gillmor, padding SHOULD be performed following the Block-Length Padding strategy. Clients SHOULD pad queries to the closest multiple of 128 octets. If a server receives a query that includes the EDNS(0) Padding option, it MUST pad the corresponding response, as specified in Section 4 of RFC 7830, and SHOULD pad the corresponding response to a multiple of 468 octets. The recommendation applies only if the DNS transport is encrypted.

In Block-Length Padding, a sender pads each message so that its padded length is a multiple of a chosen block length. This creates a greatly reduced variety of message lengths. An implementor needs to consider that even the zero-length Padding option increases the length of the packet by 4 octets.

For queries, values between 16 and 128 octets were discussed before the empirical research was performed, and responses require larger block sizes. Very large block lengths have confidentiality properties similar to the maximal-length strategy, since almost all messages fit into a single block. Such very large block length values are 288 bytes for the query, the maximum size of a one-question query over TCP without any EDNS(0) options, and the EDNS(0) buffer size of the server for responses.

The advantage of this policy is that it is reasonably easy to implement, reduces the variety of message fingerprint sizes significantly, and does not require a source of pseudo-random numbers, since the padding length required can be derived from the actual, unpadded message. Its disadvantage is that, given an unpadded message and the block size of the padding, which is assumed to be public knowledge once a server is reachable, the size range of a padded message can be predicted, so the minimum length of the unpadded message can be inferred.

The cited research performed a simulation of padding based on real-world DNS traffic captured on busy recursive resolvers of a research network. It evaluated each policy with a cost to attacker function, the percentage of query and response pairs falling into the same size bucket, and a cost to defender function, the size factor between padded and unpadded messages. Padding with a block size of 128 bytes on the query side and 468 bytes on the response side was considered the optimum trade-off. The response block size of 468 was chosen so that 3 blocks of 468 octets would still comfortably fit into typical Maximum Transmission Unit size values.

The block size interacts with the MTU size. Unless the block length is chosen so that a multiple just fits into the MTU, Block-Length Padding may cause unnecessary fragmentation for UDP-based delivery, and choosing a block length larger than the MTU always forces fragmentation. The document also notes that once DNSSEC-validating clients become more prevalent, observed size patterns are expected to change significantly, and the recommended strategy might need to be revisited.
sections.plainLanguage: Block-length padding rounds each message up to a fixed block size: 128 bytes for a question, 468 bytes for an answer. The result is that only a handful of different sizes are ever seen on the wire, so an observer cannot tell a short query from a long one. It needs no random numbers, so the padding length is simply worked out from the real message length.

sections.title: Other Strategies, Including Ones to Avoid
sections.content:
Maximal-Length Padding pads every message to the maximum size allowed by protocol negotiations. Combined with an encrypted transport it gives the highest possible level of message-size confidentiality, but it is wasteful and requires resources on the client, all intervening networks and equipment, and the server. Depending on the negotiated size it will commonly exceed the MTU and result in a consistent number of fragments, reducing delivery probability when datagram-based transport such as UDP is used. Because of the resource consumption, Maximal-Length Padding is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Random-Length Padding pads each message with a random amount of padding. Due to the size of the Padding option itself, each message size is increased by at least 4 octets, and the upper limit for padding is the maximum message size, although a client or server may choose a lower maximum. Theoretically this should create a natural distribution of message sizes, but it lets an attacker who can observe a large number of requests infer the length of the original value from the distribution of total lengths. According to the limited empirical data available, it exposes slightly more entropy to an attacker than Block-Length Padding, so it is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Random-Block-Length Padding combines Block-Length Padding with a random component: the sender randomly chooses between a few block length values and then applies Block-Length Padding based on the chosen block length. The random selection might even be based on a weak source of randomness, such as the transaction ID of the message. It creates more variety in the resulting message sizes for a certain individual original message length, but requires more implementation effort than simple Block-Length Padding, and needs further empirical study.

Two further strategies are listed in an appendix as not sensible. No Padding does not use the option at all, so the original size of the message remains unchanged and no additional confidentiality is gained; it MUST NOT be used unless message size disallows the use of the Padding option, that is, unless fewer than 4 octets are left. Fixed-Length Padding adds a constant amount of padding, which is very easy to implement and at least makes the message length differ from the original, but the amount of padding is easily discoverable from a single unencrypted message or by observing message patterns, so it is almost as useless as no padding and MUST NOT be used except for test applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The alternatives all cost something. Padding everything to the maximum size hides the most but wastes bandwidth and causes fragmentation. Padding by a random amount wastes bandwidth too and still leaks the original size through the shape of the distribution. Padding by a fixed amount leaks the amount immediately. The RFC recommends the block-length policy and rules the others out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The choice of the right padding policy, and the right parameters for the chosen policy, has a significant impact on the resilience of encrypted DNS against size-based correlation attacks. Any implementor of the Padding option must carefully consider which policies to implement, the default policy chosen, which parameters to make configurable, and the default parameter values.

No matter how carefully a client selects its padding policy, the effort can be jeopardized if the server chooses to apply an ineffective padding policy to the corresponding response packets. A client applying the Padding option may therefore want to choose a DNS server that applies a padding policy on responses that is at least equally effective.

The document also notes that even with encryption and padding, it might be trivial to identify that the observed traffic is DNS. Padding does not prevent information leaks via other side channels, particularly timing information and the number of query and response pairs. Countermeasures against such side channels could include injecting artificial cover traffic into the stream of DNS messages or delaying DNS responses by a certain amount of jitter, but such strategies are out of the scope of the document, and there is not enough theoretic analysis or experimental data available to recommend any such countermeasures.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Padding only hides one thing, the size. It does not hide when a reply arrives or how many questions were asked, and the traffic can still be recognized as DNS. Those leaks need different countermeasures, which this RFC leaves open.

viz.caption: THREE CONSTRAINTS ON ANY PADDING POLICY

items.title: EDNS(0) options space
items.text: The Padding option must be applied last, so it does not take space away from the other options.

items.title: Resource conservation
items.text: On a small device or a costly link, the extra bytes must be worth the privacy gain.

items.title: Transport independence
items.text: The size used for padding must exclude the 2 extra octets TCP adds, so both transports give the same result.

viz.caption: THE PADDING STRATEGIES AND THE RFC'S VERDICT ON EACH
